To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phytolith evidence indicates that grass-dominated habitats became common in Turkey and adjacent areas by the Early Miocene, > 7 Ma before hipparionines reached Europe and aridity ensued, as judged from the faunal evidence.

the presence of open-habitat pooid grasses in Miocene fluvial sediments in Turkey and Iran is confirmed by phytolith analysis, that the presence of C4 grasses in the Mediterranean is rare during the Miocene, and that grass-dominated ecosystems in the eastern Mediterranean are not associated with the arrival of hipparions.

the presence of grassland phytoliths in Miocene faunal localities from Turkey and Greece suggests that grasslands were present at least as early as the Early Miocene, and that the Late Miocene assemblage indicates the presence of grasslands and a reduction in forest cover, which may be related to aridification of the region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spread of grass-dominated vegetation in Turkey and surrounding regions during the Cenozic.
the early evolution of grasslands and savanna-like habitats in the eastern Mediterranean and the role of grassland expansion in the Late Miocenecenozoic mammalian faunal turnover in this region.
the spread of grass-dominated vegetation and its implications for ungulate evolution in the Miocene of Turkey, Iran, and Greece.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spread of open grass-dominated habitats in Europe and Asia Minor during the Cenozic period was not synchronous, and that the arrival of hipparions and other open-habitat ungulates in the eastern Mediterranean did not signal an abrupt change in vegetation structure, but rather an increase in landscape openness.
grasslands did not become common in Turkey until the Late Miocene.
grasslands were already widespread in Turkey and surrounding regions by the Early Miocene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spread of grass-dominated ecosystems in the eastern Mediterranean was a long-term phenomenon, not a short-term event.
the expansion of grassland habitats in Turkey and adjacent areas during the Ceno-zoic was not synchronous with that of hipparionines and arid conditions in the Mediterranean.

the grass-dominated savanna-like ecosystems in Turkey were already well developed in the Early Miocene, and the arrival of hipparions and other savanna-adapted mammals in Europe was a response to the westward extension of the grasslands in Asia Minor, rather than a cause.
The main takeaway from our work is that
grass-dominated habitats were widespread in Turkey by 20 Ma, and that their spread to Europe occurred earlier and more rapidly than previously thought.
grasslands and savannas were established in Turkey and surrounding regions during the Early Miocene.
the expansion of grass-dominated habitats was an early event in the Mediterranean region, and that it was not directly linked to faunal change in this area.
